labels.og_answer: Ankylosaurus was about 6 to 8 m (20 to 26 ft) long, and the one tail club found is about half a metre wide

top.answer: Ankylosaurus was about 6 to 8 m (20 to 26 ft) long, by a 2017 study. The smallest known Ankylosaurus came to about 4.8 tonnes (3.6 to 6 by the study's own spread), worked out from how thick its leg bones are. Our Ankylosaurus is built at that animal's size: 6.4 m (21 ft) long, almost four people lying head to foot. Its back is highest over the hips, at 1.7 m (5.6 ft), the height of the person beside it.
top.answer_more: Only one Ankylosaurus tail club has been found so far, on that same animal. Its knob is about half a metre (1.6 ft) wide, at the end of a tail whose back half was stiff as a rod.

paras: The club's knob is 60 cm (2 ft) long, 49 cm wide and only 19 cm high, measured on the fossil. It is a low, flat, rounded disc of bony plates with no spikes, and oddly no wider than the biggest clubs of its smaller relatives. The handle was the back half of the tail, its vertebrae locked together and bound by bony tendons into a stiff rod.

Only the front of the tail could bend, mostly sideways: a study of relatives' tails found a swing of about 100 degrees. Could the club break bone? In that study's model only knobs over 50 cm wide hit hard enough, and this one sits just under that line.

The best clue to its use is a study of an older relative, Zuul, with healed, broken plates on its flanks just where another club would land. So clubs seem to have served mostly in fights within their own kind. The same study has little doubt they could also fend off a predator, but no Ankylosaurus fossil shows either.

Ankylosaurus wore bony plates set in its skin, with skin between them, not a solid shell, and two bony half collars over the neck. Loose plates of its own are known, yet no Ankylosaurus has been found with a plate still in place.

So the place of each plate is a careful guess from relatives, and ours follows a 2017 plan. The big shoulder spikes of old pictures belong to another armoured family, and in its relatives the belly had no big plates. No colour is known, so ours is a choice.

blocks.nav: Ankylosaurus fossils and skeleton: what was found
blocks.h: Ankylosaurus fossils and skeleton: what was found
paras: Ankylosaurus is known from two partial skeletons and a single big skull, none complete. The first, the skeleton its name rests on, was found in 1906 in Montana by a team under Barnum Brown. His team found the second in 1910 on the Red Deer River in Alberta: AMNH 5214, the one with the club. Both are kept at the American Museum of Natural History in New York.

The biggest skull came to light in 1947, also in Alberta, and is kept at the Canadian Museum of Nature in Ottawa. The rest is loose plates, a piece of a club handle and teeth. Ankylosaurus is rare in the rocks: in one count of big dinosaurs in Montana's Hell Creek Formation, only 2 of about 180 skeletons were Ankylosaurus.
Our skeleton picture shows which bones were found with that animal.

scale.what: Our Ankylosaurus as a skeleton, to the same scale, each bone coloured by where it comes from.
scale.alt: Our Ankylosaurus as a skeleton from the side, beside the grey person, its bones in three colours by where they come from. In the colour of the bones found with this animal: the skull, jaws, both upper arm bones, a thigh bone, a calf bone, a foot bone, part of an ischium, six ribs, and the club's knob with the back of its handle.

key.text: From other Ankylosaurus finds, scaled to its size

key: Mirror copies of the other side are the right thigh bone, the top of the right ischium (a hip bone), the left calf bone and one foot bone. The plates have Ankylosaurus's own shapes, set in places guessed from relatives.

paras: The head was low and triangular, wider than long, with four short horns at its back corners. Its nostrils sat on the sides of the snout and faced down, hidden from the front, unlike in its relatives. Inside, the air probably took a looping path, a heat exchanger in models of its relatives, but what this odd nose was for is not known.

subs.h: The beak, the teeth and the food
paras: In front was a horny beak, then rows of very small, leaf-shaped teeth, 34 to 36 in each upper jaw. In the skull ours is built on, the biggest is about 9 mm high, tiny for an animal of nearly 5 tonnes. It probably ate low plants, perhaps ferns and shrubs, but its exact food is not known.

Ankylosaurus and T. rex lived at the same time in the same land, and their bones lie in the same rocks. Yet no known fossil shows the two meeting: no T. rex bite on an Ankylosaurus bone, no club wound on a T. rex. Who would win has no answer in the rocks.

What can be said: a large T. rex was about twice as heavy, about 8 to 9 tonnes against about 4.8 for the smallest known Ankylosaurus, the one ours is built on. Ankylosaurus wore plates and could swing a club, though its relatives seem to have used theirs mostly on each other.
In our picture the highest point of our Ankylosaurus stays below our T. rex's knee.

scale.what: Our T. rex, Ankylosaurus and Stegosaurus to one scale with the person, for size only. Stegosaurus lived about 80 million years earlier, and no known fossil shows Ankylosaurus and T. rex meeting.
scale.alt: Three dinosaurs from the side, all facing the same way: a T. rex on two legs, much longer and higher, the low, armoured Ankylosaurus, and a Stegosaurus with tall plates along its back, beside the grey person.

marks.text: Our T. rex, after SUE, about 11 m
Our Stegosaurus, after Sophie, about 5.6 m

paras: They never met: about 80 million years lie between them. Stegosaurus lived in the Late Jurassic, about 150 million years ago, so Ankylosaurus lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus. People pair them as armoured plant eaters, related within one larger family tree.

Ankylosaurus lived in western North America, in what is now Alberta, Saskatchewan, Montana and Wyoming, from about 68 million years ago until near the end of the Cretaceous, about 66 million years ago. The collapse that ended it is thought to have been set off by an impact in the Yucatán.

rows.text: German sites often give it a greater length and a lower weight than the figures here, without a source. The figures here come from the one modern study, of 2017: about 6 to 8 m (20 to 26 ft) for the known animals, about 4.8 tonnes for the smallest.
The upper end for the biggest animals, judged from the biggest skull. The smaller animal ours is built on was most likely near 6 m.
Calculated from the biggest skull with the same method as the smaller animal's length, from relatives' tails, and called probably too long by its own authors.
A rough scaling for the biggest skull, which has no body, and its own authors ask for caution.

rows.term: A bone-breaking club that killed T. rex
rows.text: No known T. rex bone carries a club wound, and the one Ankylosaurus knob known sits just under the size that could break bone in a model of relatives' clubs.
Old pictures borrowed them from another family of armoured dinosaurs.

rows.term: A spiked ball at the tail's end
rows.text: The only knob found is a low, flat disc, 19 cm high, with no spikes.
The 2017 study calls Ankylosaurus the biggest known ankylosaurid, and possibly the biggest ankylosaur of all.
An image, not a finding. Ankylosaurus's plates sat apart in flexible skin, and in its relatives the belly had no big plates.

blocks.intro: For each picture: where it came from, and what we know now.

rows.term: A tail lying on the ground
rows.text: Pictures and models of the early and middle 1900s showed it so. The locked bones and bony tendons of its tail say it was most likely held straight out, clear of the ground.

Park models and dioramas show them, but the plates thought to come from its flanks are squarish, with only a low ridge, and none is a tall spike. We know their shapes, but not exactly where each one sat.
That came with the old idea of a shell. The curve of its ribs and a relative's skeleton from Mongolia point to a body most likely wide, low and flat, wider than it was deep.

rows.term: Legs sprawled out to the sides, like a lizard's
rows.text: Old skeleton mounts stood it that way. Relatives' leg bones and the tracks of its family say the legs most likely stood under the body, the elbows bent only a little outward.

rows.term: Bony rings around the hips and tail
rows.text: The first restoration, in 1908, put its bony half collars there, partly after the ringed tails of glyptodonts, giant extinct relatives of armadillos. Relatives found with their armour in place show that they belong over the neck and shoulders.

items.a: About 4.8 tonnes for the animal ours is built on, the smallest Ankylosaurus known, worked out from its leg bones. The study's own spread runs from 3.6 to 6 tonnes.

items.q: What does the name Ankylosaurus mean?
items.a: Fused lizard, says the Natural History Museum in London, after bones that grew together. Barnum Brown, who also led the first find of T. rex, gave the full name, Ankylosaurus magniventris, in 1908.
No height measured on a real Ankylosaurus has been published. Ours, built up from its bones, is 1.7 m (5.6 ft) at the top of the back over the hips, its highest point.

paras: Museum of Ages is a digital museum, made by a nonprofit. Free entry, no account. In the animal wing this animal will stand among the others, from the giants of long ago to the last of their kind. The Leonardo da Vinci wing shows what a finished wing looks like.

items.line: A large adult T. rex was about 12 m long, about 4 m at the hips and roughly 8 to 9 tonnes. Our T. rex is built to SUE's measurements and stands beside a person to one scale, with a list of what was found of SUE.

items.alt: Our Triceratops from the side, 6.9 m (23 ft) from beak to tail and 2.5 m (8 ft) high over the hips: a wide frill behind the head, two long horns over the eyes, a short one on the nose, four legs. Beside it a grey person 1.70 m tall who reaches about two thirds of the way up its back.
items.line: A big adult Triceratops was about 7 to 8 m long, with a skull about 2 m. Our Triceratops is built after the Washington skeleton, a mount of about ten animals, and stands beside a person to one scale, with Torosaurus and what the bones say about T. rex.

items.alt: Our seven dinosaurs in a row from the side, to one scale. The longest, our Argentinosaurus, is about 30.6 m (100 ft) long. Two long necks tower over the rest, and a grey person 1.70 m tall looks tiny beside them.
items.line: Seven of ours beside a person, to one scale: the heaviest most likely a titanosaur from Patagonia, the tallest probably Sauroposeidon, and why the longest is still open.

items.alt: Our Stegosaurus from the side, 5.6 m (18 ft) from beak to tail tip, its back 1.9 m (6.4 ft) high over the hips: a small low head, two rows of tall plates along the arched back, two of its four tail spikes, the front legs shorter than the hind legs. Beside it a grey person 1.70 m tall whose head stays below the top of its back.
items.line: Sophie in London, an almost complete Stegosaurus, is about 5.6 m long, and a model of its skeleton gives about 1.6 tonnes. Our Stegosaurus is built after Sophie and stands beside a person to one scale.
